newsitem.title: GERMANY: ATHLETICS-CHRISTIE KEEPS EVERYONE GUESSING AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-CHRISTIE KEEPS EVERYONE GUESSING AGAIN.

text.p: Former Olympic champion Linford Christie on Friday continued to play guessing games over whether he would compete at this year's world championships in Athens.
The 37-year-old sprinter had said that the European Cup in Munich this weekend would be his last competition in a British vest.
But on Friday he kept his options open.
Christie said a British journalist had contended recently that he had been easily beaten by Canadian Donovan Bailey, his successor as Olympic 100 metres champion.
"What's the point of going to Athens if I'm going to be beaten, I might as well stay at home," Christie told a news conference with heavy sarcasm.

But later, in more mellow mood, he said: "I can beat anybody. Donovan (Bailey) is very fit because he got ready for the million-dollar race (with Michael Johnson). But there's nobody out there that's better than me. I definitely believe that."

If Christie does compete in August's world championships it would be entirely in keeping with at least five of his previous statements, when he said he would retire only to come up with a rapid retraction.

Darren Braithwaite, one of Christie's training partners and a member of the British 4x100 metres relay squad, believes his friend will be in Athens to try to eradicate the memory of the 1996 Olympic 100 metres final in Atlanta when he was disqualified for two false starts.
"I am almost certain he will return to the world championships. He's running as well as ever," Braithwaite said.
Olympic medallists Merlene Ottey of Jamaica and Ato Bolden of Trinidad, both of whom know Christie well, have also expressed the opinion that Christie will be in Athens.
Christie did confirm that this would be his last European Cup, a competition in which he has notched a record 15 victories.
He started his phenomenal run of success with a 100 metres win a decade ago and since then has won the event on six successive occasions.
In addition he has achieved four wins in the 200 metres and led the British sprint relay team to victory four times.
Christie first became British men's team captain in 1989 when they won the European Cup for the first and, so far, only time.
However, he was optimistic that he might bow out of the event by lifting the Bruno Zauli Trophy once more.
"I think that there have been stronger teams in the past," he said, referring to the relative weakness of the German, Russian and French teams.
"However the Germans are always hard to beat -- and anybody is going to be on home territory."
